Passover (Doctrine)
PAS-oh-ver
n.
Pass over, the English translation of Hebrew pesach, “to pass over, spare,” from the action of the destroying angel who passed over the houses marked with the blood of the lamb in Egypt (Ex 12). Greek pascha renders the same.

📖 Biblical Definition

Passover is the foundational redemptive feast of Israel—the annual remembrance of the LORD’s deliverance of His people from Egypt on the night of the tenth plague, when the destroying angel passed over the houses whose lintels and door-posts were marked with the blood of the slain lamb. Exodus 12 prescribes the original observance and its perpetual memorial. The lamb was taken on the tenth day of the first month (Nisan), kept until the fourteenth day, killed in the evening, its blood applied to the door-posts and lintel, its flesh roasted with fire and eaten that same night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, the household clothed and ready for the journey, the meal eaten in haste. For I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD. And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt (Ex 12:12-13). The structural features of the doctrine are several. First, the substitution: the lamb died in place of the firstborn; the blood of the lamb stood between the destroying angel and the household marked with it; substitutionary atonement is set out at the very foundation of Israel’s national identity. Second, the appropriation: not all who saw the blood were spared, but those whose households were marked by faith in the LORD’s appointed sign; the blood applied was the means of salvation. Third, the meal: the lamb was eaten by those it had saved; the saved community was constituted by the shared feast on the substitute. Fourth, the perpetual memorial: Passover was to be kept every year as a remembrance and as a teaching ordinance: and it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service? That ye shall say, It is the sacrifice of the LORD’s passover, who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt, when he smote the Egyptians, and delivered our houses (Ex 12:26-27). Fifth, and supremely, the typological fulfillment in Christ. Paul: for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us: Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor 5:7-8). John the Baptist’s announcement: behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world (John 1:29). 1 Peter 1:18-19: redeemed not with corruptible things, as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. The Last Supper, instituted at the Passover meal, became the New Covenant memorial of the substitutionary death of the True Passover Lamb. Christ Himself was crucified at Passover, at the very hour the Passover lambs were being slain in the temple court. The Passover therefore stands at the center of biblical theology: the foundational Old Testament redemptive event prefiguring the once-for-all redemptive death of Christ, whose blood passes over every soul that has been marked by faith in His atoning work.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PASSOVER as a feast of the Jews instituted to commemorate the providential escape of the Hebrews in Egypt, when God smiting the firstborn of the Egyptians, passed over the houses of the Israelites; supremely fulfilled in Christ the Passover Lamb (1 Cor 5:7), slain at the very hour the Passover lambs were killed in the temple.

PASSOVER, n. — A feast of the Jews, instituted to commemorate the providential escape of the Hebrews in Egypt, when God smiting the firstborn of the Egyptians, passed over the houses of the Israelites whose door-posts were marked with the blood of the lamb. The paschal lamb was killed on the fourteenth day of Abib (Nisan), and eaten that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.

PASCHAL, a. — Pertaining to the passover, or to the feast of Easter.

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 12:12-13 — "For I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD. And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you..."

1 Corinthians 5:7 — "Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us."

John 1:29 — "The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world!"

Luke 22:15 — "And he said unto them, With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Passover doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the supersessionist reading that has treated the Passover as merely a Jewish historical festival superseded and discarded by Christianity (rather than as the foundational shadow whose substance is Christ)—and on the other by certain Messianic and Hebrew-roots movements that have urged Christian observance of the OT Passover as continuing covenantal obligation, against the apostolic teaching that Christ has fulfilled the feast and the Lord’s table is now the New Covenant memorial.

expand to see more

The supersessionist reading treats the Passover as merely a Jewish historical festival superseded and discarded by Christianity, with little operative connection to Christian doctrine beyond an occasional sermon illustration. The apostolic teaching is sharper. The Passover is the foundational shadow whose substance is Christ; the New Testament writers do not discard the Passover but trace its typological fulfillment in Christ’s death. Christ Himself ate the Passover with His disciples and instituted the Lord’s Supper as the New Covenant memorial in continuity with the Passover’s redemptive substance. The Christian who reads past Passover as merely Old Testament-Jewish detail has missed one of the deepest typological connections in the Bible. The recovery is the recovery of the typology: Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us; the Passover’s every detail prefigured Him; the New Covenant’s Lord’s table preserves the substance the Passover prefigured.

The opposite corruption is the Messianic and Hebrew-roots movements that have urged Christian observance of the OT Passover as continuing covenantal obligation. Some traditions have argued that Christians (Gentile and Jewish believers alike) should annually celebrate Passover in something like its OT form, with a seder, the four cups, the bitter herbs, the unleavened bread, and so on. The apostolic teaching does not warrant this. Christ has fulfilled the Passover; the Lord&rsquo>s Supper instituted at the Last Supper is the New Covenant memorial; the apostolic church across the NT does not observe a continuing Passover separate from the Lord’s table; Paul explicitly rebukes the imposition of Old Covenant feast-keeping on Gentile believers (Gal 4:10; Col 2:16-17, let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ). The Christian celebration of Passover’s substance happens at every observance of the Lord’s Supper; the substance is Christ; the OT Passover is fulfilled. Recover both ends. Refuse the supersessionist reading that discards the Passover as discarded-Jewish-festival, and refuse the imposition of OT Passover observance on Christians whose new covenant memorial is the Lord’s table. The biblical doctrine traces the Passover’s substance through to Christ and finds the New Covenant fulfillment at the bread-and-cup of His own institution.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pesach (to pass over, spare); Greek pascha; the foundational redemptive feast of Israel commemorating the LORD’s deliverance from Egypt by the blood of the lamb on the lintels and door-posts; typologically fulfilled in Christ our Passover (1 Cor 5:7), whose blood passes over every soul marked by faith in His atoning work.

expand to see more

Hebrew pesach (H6453) — passover; the Hebrew name of the feast.

Hebrew pāsach (H6452) — to pass over (the verb of the LORD’s passing-over of the marked households).

Greek pascha (G3957) — passover (29 NT uses).

Greek amnos (G286) — lamb (John 1:29, the Lamb of God; 1 Pet 1:19, lamb without blemish and without spot).
